Ajahn, what is the main teaching you explore in this talk on 'this Dhamma reflection'?

In this talk, Ajahn Sumedho begins with the observation: *"[Music] So the one time I won't turn to Satan. So this afternoon you're assemble here to reflect on the way it is the dharma. I'm not a teacher. I don't want to teach you anything but point the way. And that's the basic value of Buddha Dama is like a for noble truth. His first sermon after..."* The invitation throughout is to turn attention away from conceptual analysis and toward the direct quality of knowing itself — the luminous, non-verbal awareness that is present before thought arises. This is the heart of practice: not achieving a special state, but recognising the unconditioned peace already here as *sati* (mindfulness) itself. Rest in that natural openness.

Ajahn, how do we meet suffering (dukkha) with awareness rather than resistance?

In this talk, Ajahn addresses suffering: *"The body is a realm of feelings and suffering and fear and desire that we all experience individually."* The First Noble Truth is not pessimism — it is the courageous acknowledgement: 'This is dukkha.' When we stop fighting unpleasant experience and simply know it with kind, patient awareness (sati), the suffering diminishes naturally. The wound heals fastest when kept clean and left in open air; resisting pain only tightens the knot. Bring gentle attention to wherever tension lives in your body right now.

Ajahn, this talk mentions Nibbāna. Can you explain this in the context of practice?

In this talk, the teaching on Nibbāna — the unconditioned peace beyond birth and death arises naturally from the investigation of present experience. Rather than taking this as a concept to memorise, use it as a mirror: where do you notice nibbāna showing up right now in your body, mood, or thought? The Dhamma is not a philosophy to be studied from outside but a living reality to be seen clearly from within the laboratory of awareness. Let this teaching dissolve into direct knowing.
